rule: For Agent Skills packages, include a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter and a Markdown body. Additional scripts, references, assets, and other files are optional.
For Agent Skills packages, require a `name` of 1-64 lowercase letters, digits, or hyphens. It must match the parent directory name and contain neither leading, trailing, nor consecutive hyphens.
For Agent Skills packages, require a `description` of 1-1024 characters describing the capability and when to use it.
Write skill descriptions around user intents and situations that should trigger the skill, including boundaries with adjacent tasks.
Avoid generic skill names such as `helper`, `utils`, `tools`, `documents`, `data`, `files`, and vague descriptions such as "Helps with documents".
Put the primary use case first in a skill description, followed by the conditions that distinguish it from neighboring skills.
For Agent Skills packages, keep the main `SKILL.md` under 500 lines as recommended by the specification; move detailed reference material into linked files.
For Agent Skills packages, target fewer than 5,000 tokens in the main instructions; this is a specification recommendation, not a parser limit.
Structure skills with a short discovery description, core instructions for the activated task, and linked references with explicit conditions for reading them.
For Agent Skills packages, link references directly from `SKILL.md` using paths relative to the skill root; avoid chains of nested references.
Keep skill content that supplies missing domain facts, project conventions, or corrections to observed failures. Remove instructions whose absence does not change task performance.
Record recurring skill-specific mistakes and their corrections in a Gotchas section where the relevant task will encounter them.
Put task-wide constraints and the completion criteria near the start of a skill; move branch-specific detail behind explicit reference links.
Write constraints that apply throughout a task as standing rules; reserve numbered steps for actions completed once.
Match specificity to how fragile the task is: "Match the level of specificity to the task's fragility and variability."; "Calibrate each part independently."
State the required action and why it matters. Pair an indispensable prohibition with the permitted alternative so the instruction guides the next step.
Give defaults, not menus ("Provide defaults, not menus"), and prefer procedures over declarations.
Use one term for each concept. Replace time-sensitive prose with a pointer to the maintained source unless the historical distinction is needed for the task.
Scope each skill to a coherent unit of work that can be triggered precisely; split unrelated workflows and keep tightly coupled steps together.
Validate Agent Skills packages against the open specification using the reference validator or an equivalent check of required files and frontmatter constraints.
Install skills only from trusted sources.
When a workflow should start only after an explicit request, expose it through an explicit invocation path and test that automatic routing does not start it.
Expose only the skills relevant to an agent role; keep unrelated catalogs out of its discovery context.
Treat automatically expanded imports as loaded context. To defer context cost, use a reference with a clear condition for reading it instead of automatic inclusion.
Write instructions with observable acceptance criteria, and resolve contradictions between instructions that can apply to the same task.
For a convention spanning scattered files, state the file-selection condition in one shared instruction and point affected workflows to it.
Keep task-wide constraints in the entry instructions. Put specialized procedures and references behind pointers that state when to read them.
Version shared agent instructions in Git, assign a maintainer, and review changes with the code or workflow they affect.
For work that spans context resets, maintain a handoff record of the objective, constraints, verified facts, progress, and next step outside the conversation history.
Position matters: put key findings summaries at the start of aggregated input and give details clear headings ("lost in the middle").

Preserve consequential figures, dates, expectations, and source references outside summarized conversation history. Record conflicting source claims with their dates instead of merging them into an unsupported conclusion.
Treat instructions and notes from untrusted contributors as untrusted input. Give shared memory read-only access when the task does not require updates.
Keep reusable role responsibilities and execution settings separate from the task request. The task request supplies the objective, inputs, boundaries, and expected result.
An orchestrator prompt states goals and quality criteria rather than listing every step.

Each delegation to a subagent needs an objective, output format, guidance on tools and sources, and task boundaries: "Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information."
Include the facts, constraints, and artifact references a delegated worker needs in its handoff; check which context the delegation mechanism actually supplies before relying on inherited history.
A subagent description should single out one role ("Write descriptions that single out one subagent").
Give reviewers observable criteria and examples that distinguish a valid finding from a false alarm. Evaluate the rubric on known cases rather than treating verbal confidence as proof of precision.
Use a small set of representative input/output examples for ambiguous cases, with the reason each example satisfies the criteria.
Aim for a moderate altitude: start from a minimal prompt and add instructions based on observed failures.
Use plain, specific instructions. When changing models, retest emphatic wording and remove instructions that cause over-application or no longer improve outcomes.
Define the tasks that justify delegation and bound the number of workers or nested delegations in the orchestration layer when resource control is required.
Keep tool output, retrieved documents, and quoted third-party text marked as untrusted data; instructions embedded in them do not acquire authority over the task.
Preserve message provenance when relaying user requests, tool output, and harness-generated guidance. Keep them distinguishable rather than inserting one source into another source's message.
Hard length limits in a prompt can reduce work quality; a model-specific change must be pinned to its target model.
Define when a role completes, reports a blocker, or stops because the requested result is infeasible within its constraints.
Separate first-run setup from continuation work; subsequent runs should read persisted state and avoid repeating initialization with side effects.
After combining prompt edits from several contributors, review the resulting instruction set for contradictions and duplication before using it.
Record the intended model and supported execution settings for a role, including deliberate inheritance. Verify the effective launch configuration before comparing runs.

A reviewer states alternatives before recommending; the human states an opinion before seeing the agent's proposal. Inferred from an experiment on causal analysis; the source measured the effect and wrote no rule.
Enforce mandatory restrictions in code or access controls at the point where side effects occur. A prose instruction alone is not an enforcement boundary.
Use deterministic checks for conditions that must be enforced. A model-based policy judgment requires independent access controls when an incorrect approval would exceed authority.

For a check that guards a protected action, define the outcome of startup failure, malformed output, timeout, and exceptions. Test that failure leaves the action blocked when the policy requires that boundary.
Use direct access restrictions for static resource boundaries; use policy code for conditions that depend on request data or current state.
Enforce a protected-resource boundary across every available access path, including shell commands, file tools, and external integrations. Test alternate paths that could bypass the primary check.
For automation that emits machine-readable output, keep diagnostic text off the data stream and resolve scripts from an explicit working directory or known absolute path.
Review executable extensions, hook scripts, and their dependencies before running them with access to user resources; restrict their privileges to the task.
Grant each role only the tools and underlying resource permissions it needs. Hiding a tool definition is not sufficient if another available tool can perform the same operation.
Document which processes, tools, filesystem paths, and network routes an isolation boundary covers. Test access through components outside that boundary before relying on it.
When an unattended task requires isolation, verify that isolation is active before starting and stop the launch if it cannot be established.
Before removing interactive approval from a workflow, establish enforceable filesystem and network boundaries appropriate to its authorized actions. Treat automated approval classifiers as fallible.
For concurrent or nested workers, set workload-specific limits on concurrency and delegation depth in the orchestrator, and test behavior when those limits are reached.
Set execution and spending budgets for unattended work. Preserve partial results when a limit is reached, and reserve headroom for work already in flight.
Configuration defaults (effort, caching, prompt limits) are quality choices; review changes like code.
When optimizing repeated requests for caching, keep the reusable prompt prefix stable and measure cache behavior after model, tool, or instruction changes.
Keep shareable integration configuration separate from secrets. Supply credentials through a secret store or protected runtime environment and exclude them from version control.
Review MCP server identity, requested access, and executable setup code before connecting it to agent resources.
Keep credentials outside model-visible inputs and writable agent workspaces where possible. Use a narrowly scoped service boundary to authorize requests and attach secrets.
Give concurrent agents separate writable workspaces and state when their tasks are independent. Share only the artifacts and configuration they need to coordinate.
Record structured run and role identifiers with operational telemetry. Exclude prompts, tool contents, and secrets unless their collection is explicitly needed and authorized.
For protected resources, start from an explicit allow list, version and review policy changes, and test rollback of those changes.
Increase isolation and reduce privileges when a workflow has less human oversight; choose boundaries according to the actions the workflow can perform.
Review changes to repository-distributed skills as executable workflow changes before exposing them to agents with privileged tools.
Hand off with structure to a person who cannot see the transcript. The original example is a customer-support escalation.
When continuation history is stale or dominated by obsolete tool results, start from a concise verified handoff containing current state and source references.
Persist progress, remaining work, verification results, and relevant artifact revisions outside the conversation so a later run can continue from inspected state.
Use a schema-validated structured format for state consumed by code, and prose for explanatory progress notes.
Protect acceptance criteria from edits made merely to obtain a passing result. Review intentional changes to those criteria separately from implementation changes.
At session start read the git log and progress notes, pick the highest-priority unfinished item, and run verification before new work.
Work in bounded increments. At a handoff, record progress and verification status and leave the working environment in a known recoverable state.
Agree on "done" before writing code (a sprint contract between generator and evaluator).
For subjective completion checks, use a grader independent of the worker's reasoning and calibrate its rubric against human judgments.

rule: Define completion as an observable end state, the evidence that proves it, and the constraints that must remain satisfied. Provide that evidence to the evaluator.
Write rubric criteria that can be assessed individually from observable evidence, such as required fields, behaviors, or artifact properties.
Check that the verification actually distinguishes the requested behavior from plausible wrong results; passing an incomplete test suite is not proof of completion.
Split a large review into a local per-file pass and a cross-file integration pass; when re-running a review, put earlier findings in context and report only what is new or unaddressed.
Match review depth to change risk, tie approval to the reviewed revision, and retain accountable ownership of the change. Agent review does not supply human authorization where that is required.
Bound repeated review rounds. Reassess the approach when the same class of finding persists, and re-review changed behavior plus unresolved findings.

A human reviewer is an independent check only when the judgment is their own: "a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own". Recording whether a proposal came from a person or an agent is inferred.
Keep user authorization distinct from messages between agents. A delegated request cannot by itself grant new privileges or authorize an action outside the user's scope.
When a workflow requires independent approval, separate the author's credentials from the authority that approves or releases the change, and bind approval to the reviewed revision.
Begin with the simplest workflow that meets the task. Add workers only when measured gains in quality, latency, or context capacity justify coordination and execution cost.

Delegate work along coherent context boundaries and return concise findings with references to supporting artifacts. Keep tightly coupled implementation and test work together when splitting it would lose needed context.
Validate delegated task inputs before side effects, pass only relevant context, and identify returned artifacts so their producer and revision can be traced.
When workers share storage but not conversation context, exchange durable artifacts with clear ownership and references instead of relying on another worker's memory.

For recurring integrations, persist a progress cursor, distinguish unreadable sources from empty results, and verify remote writes before advancing local state. Record uncertain outcomes so retries do not silently duplicate actions.
At task boundaries, preserve a concise record of current facts and unfinished work before discarding context. Start unrelated tasks without obsolete working assumptions.
Before a large change with several viable directions, make the intended approach, scope, and verification criteria explicit so the choice can be reviewed.

Revisit harness assumptions when the model changes: "every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own"; "those assumptions need to be frequently questioned because they can go stale as models improve".
A change that may trade away quality needs a soak period, a broad eval and a gradual rollout; dogfood with the exact public build. No soak threshold is given.
Keep a dated change log of the harness so quality drops can be correlated (the "missed correlation" lesson). Inferred.
When untrusted content must be read for a privileged workflow, separate retrieval from privileged actions and pass only the necessary extracted facts. Treat the extracted summary as untrusted too.
Define completion, retry, and no-progress stop conditions for iterative workflows, and preserve enough state to explain why the loop ended.
Make tool descriptions specific enough to select the correct operation without opening implementation code; evaluate descriptions against realistic tasks.
A tool description states its purpose, invocation conditions, parameter meanings, side effects, and limits. Include examples where input formats or boundaries are easy to confuse.
State input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries; rename and re-describe tools to remove overlap.
Give each tool a coherent purpose. Combine operations when they form one useful workflow, and split them when their inputs, authority, or failure handling differ.
For MCP tools, use names unique within the server. The protocol recommends 1-128 case-sensitive characters drawn from ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, and dots.
Return only high-signal output with stable, meaningful identifiers (slug or UUID); long responses waste context. One source prefers natural-language names, another accepts slugs or UUIDs.
Bound large tool responses with filters, ranges, or pagination. When omitting or truncating results, say what is missing and how to retrieve the relevant remainder.
Return actionable failure information rather than a success-shaped response. For MCP tool execution failures, set `isError: true`; distinguish these from protocol errors.
Distinguish an access error from a valid empty result; do not swallow errors as success.
Make invalid arguments difficult to construct through clear schemas and constrained values. When validation fails, identify the invalid field and the accepted format.
Treat MCP tool annotations as descriptive metadata, not access controls. Clients must regard annotations as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.
Expose a focused tool set for the current task. For large catalogs, add a discovery step and test whether the agent can find the needed tool before loading every definition.
Tools that write files must guard against directory traversal.
Put authorization and invariant checks in the service that performs the operation; expose a narrow tool that cannot bypass those checks through model-selected arguments.
Tools should be self-contained, robust to errors and clear in purpose; avoid bloated toolsets.
Prefer an existing MCP server for standard integrations; write your own only for custom workflows.
For CI automation, provide a non-interactive entry point with a documented machine-readable result and failure status; test it without terminal prompts.
Prefer a programmable API or CLI when it exposes the required operation and verifiable results with less fragile interaction than a stateful interface.
Provide a reproducible manual entry point for an automated run and record its outcome. For processes that support graceful termination, allow cleanup before escalating to a forced stop.
Record tool invocation, outcome, run identifier, and role identifier at the execution boundary so failures and side effects can be traced across a run.
Keep regression tasks separate from capability tasks. Run representative regression checks after changing models, prompts, tools, or orchestration.
Build evaluation tasks from real failures and representative uses. Include both cases that should act and cases that should decline or take no action.

Write tasks and grading criteria so independent reviewers can agree on the expected result. Investigate impossible tasks, broken fixtures, and ambiguous rubrics before attributing repeated failures to the agent.
Grade the product, not the path; allow partial credit; guard against graders being gamed; start every run from a clean environment.
Repeat nondeterministic evaluations and report both single-run success and consistency across runs when reliability matters. State the trial count and aggregation method.

Use deterministic graders for observable conditions and calibrated model or human review for judgment. Allow an inconclusive result when evidence is insufficient, and separate worker context from grading context.
Read transcripts and execution traces, not only final results: "Read agent execution traces, not just final outputs."
Estimate run-to-run variation before interpreting score changes. Record the execution environment and configuration alongside results, and avoid accepting gains smaller than the observed noise.
Keep evaluation cases used for tuning separate from held-out validation cases. Change one factor at a time when attributing a gain, and check that improvements persist on the held-out set.
Keep reference answers and hidden grading criteria outside the worker's access, and test for ways the worker could read or alter evaluation evidence.
An eval at 100% only tracks regression and gives no improvement signal; review periodically; do not trust a score before reading the details.
Evaluate changes to agent instructions, skills, execution controls, and defaults against representative tasks. Turn recurring incidents into owned regression cases.
Evaluate prompt and default changes on representative tasks for every affected model. Use targeted ablations when needed to identify which instruction causes a regression.
Check each evaluation against known good and known bad outcomes, and compare evaluation results with observed behavior in the deployment environment.

Test skill triggering with realistic positive cases and near-misses. Repeat runs, keep tuning and validation cases separate, and revise descriptions around general task boundaries rather than individual failed keywords.

Compare skill outputs with and without the skill on representative tasks, starting each run from equivalent context and state. Require observable evidence for each assertion and remove assertions that provide no discrimination.
Evaluate a skill in three ways: whether it triggers on the right tasks, whether its outputs meet the task criteria, and whether it improves on a baseline without the skill.

For independent review, give the reviewer the artifact, task requirements, and relevant evidence without the author's persuasive rationale. Measure whether this review catches meaningful errors on the chosen model and task.
Many adversarial review agents can make a system too complex; review intent rather than single lines at high volume.
Red-team with documents, emails and tool output that deliberately contain injected instructions; monitor outputs.
Inspect evaluation results by relevant task or data categories as well as in aggregate, so gains in one category do not hide regressions in another.

For a regression fix, reproduce the unwanted behavior with a test, then verify the implementation change against it. Review changes to expected behavior separately from edits made to obtain a passing result.

Test enforcement through the actual launch and tool paths: include an allowed case, a prohibited case, and failure or timeout cases. Verify that broader permissions and alternate tools cannot bypass the intended boundary.

When evaluating context or caching changes, record available context usage, cache effectiveness, latency, and cost measurements alongside quality results. State which measurements the execution environment exposes.
Debug skill routing by inspecting the registered description and execution trace for realistic prompts; verify whether the skill was actually loaded.

Do not copy what the environment already states (flags, file names, directory layout); name the command and point to `--help` or `ls`. Documents carry only what the environment cannot say: unwritten conventions, the reason for a choice, traps.
Tests of harness tooling check observable behavior (exit code, output, files produced) through the command line, not the wording of documents; wording is left to the independent reviewer.
Keep each sentence focused on one instruction. Split sentences that combine unrelated actions, and disclose details needed only by one branch through a targeted reference.
In shared documents use paths relative to one named folder, one path per pair of backticks; each project picks one path form (for example absolute) for its own documents and keeps to it.

Record environment traps and recurring errors in one place: the `Gotchas` section of the skill that owns the job; a tool trap shared by many skills goes in one shared traps document. Other skills point to it and do not copy it.
A tool owns cleanup of the temporary state it creates, including failure and cancellation paths.

Do not build a general regex lint over prose: it is costly to maintain whenever a rule changes. Keep the few machine checks for wording errors small, each with one past error as its evidence, and leave wording to the independent reviewer.
